noticias.titulo: Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
noticias.resumen: Disruptions at Yemen's largest seaport could exacerbate hardships for millions of Yemenis, aid experts warn.
noticias.texto:
Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
The Houthi-held seaport is a critical lifeline for millions of Yemenis but has taken significant damage over the course of recent conflicts.
The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The strikes come amid significant Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks and escalating attacks by the group on Saudi Arabia.
Hodeidah, which has repeatedly been attacked over the past decade, is critical to both Yemen’s economy and the supply of essential goods to millions of people in Houthi-controlled areas.
Here’s what we know:
How important is the port of Hodeidah?
The port of Hodeidah, situated on Yemen’s western Red Sea coast, is the country’s principal commercial seaport and has been under Houthi control since 2014.
It serves as a major entry point for food, fuel and other commercial goods as well as humanitarian assistance, supplying the densely populated northern and western regions of Yemen, including the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.
The port had eight berths and the capacity to accommodate 6,500 standard shipping containers in 2023. However, attrition due to Yemen’s more than a decade of conflict has reduced the number of operational berths and damaged cranes and storage facilities.
Despite this, in September 2025, the United Nations Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement estimated that the port handled about 70 percent of commercial imports and 80 percent of humanitarian aid coming into Yemen, calling it a “lifeline”.
“The closure or disruption [of the port] under the current circumstances would delay the arrival of food, medicine and fuel; increase transport costs and prices; and exacerbate the suffering of families already facing an acute humanitarian crisis,” said Abdusattor Esoev, Yemen Chief of Mission for the International Organization for Migration.
“At a time when millions of people in Yemen depend on humanitarian assistance and face severe food insecurity, Hodeidah remains a critical lifeline. The port is essential for bringing in food, fuel, medicines and other basic goods needed by civilians across northern Yemen,” said Francesca Quinto, the programme manager for Yemen for Doctors Without Borders.
However, the Houthis have long been accused of using Hodeidah’s port for both civilian and military purposes. Investigations have found that the group exploits commercial port facilities to smuggle in weapons from Iran, its chief ally.
“The ports of Hodeidah are key to commercial flows. However, the Houthis’ increasing militarisation of vital civilian infrastructure by smuggling and storing arms, fuel and narcotics is undermining the humanitarian functions they serve in wartime,” Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera.
Tawfiq al-Hamidi, a Yemeni lawyer and human rights activist, told Al Jazeera that the port has been misused by the group for smuggling despite its importance for Yemen’s population.
“Nevertheless, efforts must be made to protect the port as a civilian facility, and the Houthi movement must provide genuine guarantees,” he said.
Has the port been attacked before?
Yes. Since the start of Yemen’s civil war in September 2014, the port and its surrounding area have repeatedly come under attack from the Saudi-led coalition, the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. Pro-Yemeni government forces also tried to capture it in a 2018 offensive.
About 70 percent of Yemenis live in Houthi-controlled areas in the country’s west, where most goods arrive from the rest of the world through Red Sea ports. Humanitarian aid continues to enter through other ports, including Mocha and a major government-held port in Aden, but renewed fighting has made the overland flow of this aid to the country’s interior difficult. Humanitarian operations in Houthi-controlled areas have also been severely curtailed because of the detention of UN staff by the group.
In March 2015, shortly after launching its military intervention in support of the Yemeni government, the Saudi-led coalition began a partial maritime blockade on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
A UN-brokered nationwide truce in April 2022 led to an easing of restrictions on fuel imports through Hodeidah. Further restrictions on commercial imports were lifted in early 2023, which also helped to revitalise the port.
But that recovery was then jeopardised by a campaign of US, British and Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled areas beginning in 2024 and lasting into the next year, in retaliation for Houthi drone and missile attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping, carried out ostensibly in the name of supporting Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.
Why is Saudi Arabia attacking the port now?
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announced on Wednesday that it had launched new strikes against the Houthis at the port, days after it warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Houthis have promised not to let strikes against the port go unanswered.
Since the return of full-scale war to Yemen in September, the Houthis have made sweeping territorial gains across Yemen, pushing back the forces of the internationally recognised government.
A government counteroffensive launched in early October has failed to stem Houthi advances despite heavy air support. Government forces are now scrambling to defend Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“Broadly speaking, the strikes [on Hodeidah’s port] were a response to the shift on the battlefield in favour of the Houthis,” Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera.”
“They were aimed at undermining and crippling their economic and logistical capabilities, including infrastructure, such as ports and airports, as well as their military capabilities,” he said.
Escalating Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia targeting airports, oil infrastructure and commercial buildings also played a role in the decision, al-Dhahab said, mentioning Thursday’s attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh.
The following day, the Saudi-led coalition urged civilians near Hodeidah’s port to evacuate without providing specifics.
What could happen next?
Before Wednesday’s strikes, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree reiterated a threat of retaliation on Saudi seaports on the Red Sea, naming Jeddah’s port in particular.
Nabil Al-Bukairi, a Yemeni researcher and policy expert, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the port should not be taken as a warning. “I believe the strikes have gone beyond being merely symbolic,” he said.
“Continued bombardment would inevitably lead to its closure and render it inoperable once its infrastructure and logistical capabilities have been targeted,” he warned.
Even without a closure, strikes that disrupt the operations of the facility risk delays of critical aid as Yemen’s war shows no sign of an imminent end.

noticias.titulo: UK military ‘moving aircraft to hangars in case of drone attacks’
noticias.resumen: Experts say the move is a 'logical response' if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat.
noticias.texto:
UK military ‘moving aircraft to hangars in case of drone attacks’
Experts say the move is a ‘logical response’ if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it takes “the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously,” after media outlets reported the Royal Air Force (RAF) had taken new precautions against possible drone attacks.
The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday that planes would be moved to hangars and hardened shelters overnight, and anti-drone nets would be installed to protect any warplanes that remained exposed.
The MoD did not confirm the reports, but in a statement said it was “always adapting to counter any potential threats”.
Justin Bronk, a senior researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank in London, told Al Jazeera that the RAF’s reported tactics would be “a sensible, logical response if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat”.
“The main bases used for RAF fighters, Coningsby, Marham and Lossiemouth all still have hardened aircraft shelters from the Cold War era that have been maintained in usable condition for both aircraft storage, protection and limited maintenance work,” Bronk said.
However, Bronk cautioned that there were not enough hardened shelters to protect all of the jets at each airbase, after squadrons were consolidated into ‘super bases’ following the end of the Cold War, and a “mistaken assumption” that such protection was no longer important.
The MoD said it was investing an additional 470 million pounds ($615m) “to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities”, and that 15 million pounds ($19.6m) had already been invested “in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites”.
Attack readiness
British authorities have regularly issued warnings about threats posed by Russia and Iran, and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies. In a report in October, members of Parliament warned that Britain’s military needed to make “dramatic progress” to be ready for a potential attack by Russia on a NATO country.
On Tuesday, Britain’s domestic MI5 intelligence service and the MoD issued a joint alert warning UK military suppliers to Ukraine about increasing sabotage attempts by Russia.
“Aircraft inside a standard hangar or a hardened aircraft shelter are protected from attacks by infiltrated adversary cells or terrorists with small drones,” explained RUSI’s Justin Bronk. “But only those in hardened shelters are protected from larger one-way attack drones like the Geran 2/3/4 series during a hypothetical wartime attack,” he added, referring to the Geran drones manufactured and operated by Russia, based on an original Iranian design.
Bronk said that even though hardened aircraft shelters seem old-fashioned, they are a “relatively low-risk, inexpensive and effective way to improve fighter fleet resilience in wartime.”
“They provide almost total protection from drones due to thick concrete and blast doors, and also mean that any unintercepted cruise missile can only destroy a single jet at most with a direct hit.”
US withdraws military aircraft
Earlier this month US forces responded to possible unauthorised drone activity over a military base in the United Kingdom, hosting American warplanes.
“No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected” at the eastern RAF Lakenheath base, a US Air Force spokesperson said in a statement at the time.
There was also an Iran-linked security scare on September 27 at the southwestern RAF Fairford base, which was used by the US planes. A group of men allegedly drove three vans up to a village near the site and abandoned them with filled petrol barrels inside, sparking a bomb scare and evacuation.
Washington had used the airbase in its war on Iran, and days after the September incident withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base. Two men have since been charged in a UK court over the incident, and three in the United States.
The US military also withdrew its planes from RAF Mildenhall, near Lakenheath, on November 9 , following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal and The Financial Times.

noticias.titulo: US grants SpaceX approval for 1 million space data centres
noticias.resumen: Elon Musk hails FCC's approval of SpaceX's Starmind project as 'a great asset to America and the world.'
noticias.texto:
US grants SpaceX approval for 1 million space data centres
Elon Musk hails FCC’s approval of SpaceX’s Starmind project as ‘a great asset to America and the world.’
The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorised Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy a constellation of data centres in space, named “Starmind”, in a bid to help meet rapidly ‌‌growing demand ‌‌for AI computing.
The FCC said on Wednesday the approval marked a first in the history of the United States.
“At this pivotal time in America’s development of super intelligence [artificial intelligence], the FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” an FCC press release said.
“This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr in a statement.
Elon Musk praised the FCC decision on social media.
“Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” he said on X.
Approving the application will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent ‌technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence”, the FCC said.
Data centres are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power.
SpaceX filed for permission to deploy Starmind ‌earlier this year.
It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility.
SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has just more than 11,000 satellites in space.
Last month, the FCC’s Space Bureau and Wireless Telecommunications Bureau granted Space Exploration Holdings, LLC, a subsidiary of SpaceX, authority to launch and operate the SpaceX NGSO MSS System, commercially known as Starlink.
Amazon’s rival satellite unit Leo and others have criticised the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so.
Carr rejected that criticism in March.
“Amazon should focus on ‌getting Amazon’s house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the ‌pace ‌and cadence that SpaceX is,” Carr said.

noticias.titulo: World reacts to Trump’s new tariffs as US stocks tumble
noticias.resumen: The new levies come after an eight-month investigation launched by the United States Trade Representative.
noticias.texto:
World reacts to Trump’s new tariffs as US stocks tumble
The new levies come after an eight-month investigation launched by the United States Trade Representative.
The Trump administration has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union, claiming that excess production has given them an unfair advantage.
The proposed levies come after a months-long investigation into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan, launched after the Supreme Court struck down United States President Donald Trump’s sweeping global tariffs in February.
The highest tariff rate announced on Wednesday would hit China the hardest, at 20 percent, adding to the roughly 25 percent duties that Trump imposed on China during his first term.
The proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30bn of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.
Washington has long accused China of subsidising its industries and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products, allegations that Beijing has once again denied.
“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations.
Other US trading partners facing proposed new tariffs include India, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
Mexico and Norway were also part of the probe but were excluded from the new round of tariffs because investigations into their trade practices are still ongoing.
‘Cynical’ use of Section 301
The tariff announcement follows an eight-month investigation initiated by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.
“The administration’s use of Section 301 is cynical,” Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera. “It launched these investigations in order to support the president’s aim to set tariffs globally and to modify them at any time at the president’s will, and thus strip Congress of the authority to set tariff rates under the taxing power set forth in the Constitution.”
In a separate announcement, the White House also announced a proposed 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer, whose jets are widely used by US regional carriers operating under brands including United Express, Delta Connection and American Eagle. Finished aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-biggest export to the US.
The US also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices, according to a senior US official.
Global reaction
Several governments have reacted to the new tariff announcement, as has the European Union.
“The EU takes note of the publication by the US of preliminary findings pursuant to its Section 301 investigation concerning structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors,” European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Al Jazeera.
“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Gill added.
The Swiss government has also reacted, saying that it rejects the allegations stemming from the investigations.
“The timing right before the G20 [in mid-December] sets up those meetings as an opportunity for negotiation and increases risk of both inflationary pressures and macro volatility in 2027, reducing some of the benefit from easing gas prices,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
Norway has praised the decision.
“We have been clear throughout the process that Norway does not have policies that contribute to overcapacity. Norwegian companies produce in response to market demand,” Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said.
Markets react
US markets fell on news of the new tariffs.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.6 percent after tumbling more than 4 percent in early trading, while the S&P 500 closed down 0.25 percent.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.3 percent, reversing earlier losses.
The price of gold – which is considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty – fell by more than 3 percent to its lowest level in more than a year. However, in addition to tariffs, the price was influenced by inflation data released on Wednesday which showed a 0.3 percent rise in one of the US Federal Reserve’s key metrics for assessing the rate of inflation. Higher inflation increases the chances of a rise in interest rates, which in turn weighs on the metal.
Bond yields in both the US and Europe dropped on Wednesday.
Germany’s 10-year bond yield, which is the benchmark for the eurozone, slid by 4.5 basis points to 3.2 percent, while the US 10-year Treasury note yield stumbled by 6.8 basis points to 4.834 percent, putting it on pace for its seventh daily drop over the past eight sessions.

noticias.titulo: At least 30 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, health ministry says
noticias.resumen: An additional 15 were injured in blaze after vehicle carrying petroleum products flipped on a major road.
noticias.texto:
At least 30 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, health ministry says
An additional 15 were injured in blaze of fire after vehicle carrying petroleum products flipped on a major road.
At least 30 people were killed and another 25 were injured when a vehicle carrying ‌‌petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring road in the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the Health Ministry said on Wednesday.
The fire broke out above a tunnel in the Warraq neighbourhood of Giza’s Imbaba district. The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, ‌‌Giza and Qalyubia.
Local media reported that a truck swerved and hit the central reservation as it overturned, triggering an explosion. The fire has since been extinguished, according to local media.
Egypt’s public prosecutor announced an investigation into the crash and ordered the collection of DNA samples from the victims’ bodies. The judicial office also said 27 vehicles were burned.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the site of the incident and that the injured were transferred to nearby hospitals.
The official spokesman for the Egyptian presidency said that President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “expresses his sincere condolences and sincere sympathy to the families of the victims” and wished them a speedy recovery.
According to an Egyptian Cabinet statement, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly offered his condolences to the victims’ families and ordered that their medical expenses be covered by the state.
“The Ministry of Health and Population continues to closely monitor the situation and coordinate with the relevant authorities to ensure that the necessary medical care is provided to the injured,” a ministry statement read.

noticias.titulo: Nigeria’s Tinubu pledges to bring peace to rebellion-hit border region
noticias.resumen: Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that military operations in the country's northeast will deliver security.
noticias.texto:
Nigeria’s Tinubu pledges to bring peace to rebellion-hit border region
Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that intensified military operations in Borno and the northwest will deliver lasting security gains.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu promised supporters in the northeastern city of Maiduguri he would restore peace to their rebellion-hit region, as an election looms in January.
Tinubu made the pledge at a rally in the city on Wednesday, as he seeks a second and final term in an election on January 16.
Maiduguri is the capital of Borno State, the heartland of the rebellion led by Boko Haram and ISIL West Africa Province (ISWAP).
Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that intensified military operations in Borno and the northwest, where kidnapping for ransom remains rife, will deliver lasting security gains for communities scarred ‌by conflict.
“We will achieve that peace; the terrorism will go; they [rebel fighters] have the opportunity now to lay down their arms, to lay down all arms and surrender all weapons, change from the character of terrorism and banditry,” Tinubu said.
Holding the rally in Maiduguri sent a “simple statement saying there’s an improvement in the security situation”, Kabir Adamu, the managing director at Beacon Security and Innovations Limited, told Al Jazeera.
It also showed “an improvement … in the economic circumstances within the state”, Adamu said, speaking from Nigeria’s capital of Abuja.
Tinubu’s main rivals are former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, a former Anambra State governor who won more than 6 million votes in the last election.
Insecurity remains despite some progress
Ending insecurity in the north was one of Tinubu’s promises when campaigning for the presidency in 2023, but analysts and his opponents say that, like his predecessors, he has fallen short.
More than 50 percent of respondents disapprove of the president’s performance and more than 70 percent rate the economy “poor or very poor”, according to a YIAGA Africa poll released in October.
But Adamu said, “significant progress” has been made within Borno State.
“There was a time when about 24 local governments were more or less being contested, in terms of their control by the state or non-state actors,” he explained.
“Now, reasonably, almost all the local governments are accessible, even though there are challenges outside the immediate city centres.”
Nigeria’s defence minister said this month that the military was receiving real-time US intelligence and satellite support to target armed group leaders and degrade rebel networks.
In May, US and Nigerian forces led a mission that killed Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, ISIL’s global second-in-command.
Security analysts say Nigerian forces have driven rebels from most of the territory they once held, but the fighters still stage deadly raids, ambushes and bombings.
The armed groups have also been increasing their activities in the northwest, where kidnapping gangs mostly operate.
Crisis monitoring group ACLED said earlier this year that fighters ‌linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS) were rapidly increasing their attacks on the borderlands between Niger, Benin and Nigeria, turning remote transit corridors into active conflict zones.
Tinubu said security forces were working to ‌rescue ‌more than 70 schoolchildren who remain in captivity after being abducted in two separate attacks in May and June in Borno.
Another key issue in the run-up to the elections is economic reform, as poverty has increased and access to basic commodities is increasingly difficult, said Adamu.

noticias.titulo: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65
noticias.resumen: Andy Taylor first revealed he was battling cancer in 2022 when Duran Duran was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. The band had numerous hits in the 1980s, including "Girls on Film" and "Hungry Like The Wolf."
noticias.texto:
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65
November 25, 2026
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer," his family announced on Wednesday. He was 65.
Taylor was responsible for 1980s new wave hits like "Girls on Film," "Hungry Like The Wolf" and "Rio."
The band's pioneering music videos helped drive early success, including through airtime on MTV.
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music," the band said in a statement.
"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
A career atop the charts
Duran Duran accumulated a slew of accolades including two Grammys, six platinum records, two Ivor Novello Awards and the MTV Video Visionary Award.
Taylor parted with the band in 1986 to pursue other projects.
The band was due to reunite when they were inducted into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
However, Taylor was unable to be present. He revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years.
"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote at the time. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."

noticias.titulo: Egypt: At least 31 dead after fuel truck overturns on highway
noticias.resumen: The accident occurred on the packed Ring Road in Giza near Cairo. Dozens of ambulances responded to the crash, and Egyptian health authorities say the death toll could rise.
noticias.texto:
Egypt: Over 30 dead after fuel truck overturns near Cairo
November 25, 2026
A fuel truck overturned on a packed highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, killing 31 people and injuring 21 more, according to Egyptian authorities.
What do we know so far?
The fuel tanker crash ignited a massive blaze on Ring Road in Giza's Waraq district. The Ring Road encircles the greater Cairo metropolitan area.
Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were transported to nearby hospitals and added that the death toll could rise further. He said 39 ambulances are responding to the accident.
A massive fire broke out after the accident, with rescue workers pulling people from their vehicles. A large crowd gathered in the densely populated Waraq neighborhood amid the rescue efforts.
The blaze left at least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, charred.
An investigation has been launched into the crash, according to Egypt's public prosecutor. DNA tests are being carried out to identify badly burned victims of the blaze.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his deepest condolences and sympathy to the victims and directed relevant authorities to provide necessary support to the families of the victims and the injured.
Italy, Algeria extend condolences to victims
Other countries also reacted to the crash in Giza.
Italian Foreign Affairs Minister Antonio Tajani said he extended his "deepest solidarity to the victims' families," Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty "and to the Egyptian people, whom I count as friends, at this tragic time."
Algerian Ambassador to Egypt Mohamed Sofiane Berrah also said the Embassy of Algeria in Cairo extended "its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathy to the sisterly Arab Republic of Egypt."
Car accidents are frequent in Egypt due to poor road conditions, reckless driving and lax enforcement of safety rules.

noticias.titulo: Nigeria detains 5 Mexicans, confiscates over $220 million of meth
noticias.resumen: Nigeria's anti-drug agency said Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern state of Enugu.
noticias.texto:
Nigeria detains 5 Mexicans, confiscates over $220 million of meth
November 25, 2026
Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLA) said Wednesday it had arrested five Mexicans and confiscated over $220 million (around €200 million) in methamphetamine as part of a significant drug bust.
What do we know about the drug bust?
The agency said the Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern Nigerian state of Enugu.
"A total of 1,512 kilograms of methamphetamine, finished and in production, with an estimated value of $226.8 million was recovered from the clandestine factory," NDLA spokesperson Femi Babafemi said.
Nigeria first rejected the entry of the Mexicans into the country in August. They later entered Nigeria again in September via neighboring Benin using forged passports, with authorities then putting them under surveillance.
On November 11, the Mexicans were taken into custody at the Enugu lab after their movements were tracked by the Nigerian government. A Nigerian was also arrested in a nearby hotel.
The latest drug bust comes after Nigerian authorities in May also detained 10 people in a anti-meth operation in the southwest, including three Mexicans.
Why do Mexican cartels find African countries desirable for drug production?
The arrests raise concern that Mexican cartels are getting a foothold in Africa for international drug trafficking. In addition to Nigeria, South Africa is another country where Mexicans have been arrested for being involved in a meth lab.
According to Vanda Felbab-Brown, an expert at the Washington DC-based Brookings Institution, Mexican cartels such as the Sinaloa Cartel and the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generation (CJNG) have expanded their operations into other continents such as Africa.
In a June testimony to the US Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control, Felbab-Brown said the cartels find "desirable partners" for production in countries such as South Africa and Kenya due to factors such as "limited law enforcement capacities and entrenched criminal and corrupt networks."
According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime,criminal networks often take advantage of porous borders in the West and Central Africa region to carry out activities such as illicit drug trafficking.
"Many countries in the region have vast territory and borders are located either in very remote or densely populated areas, thus making law enforcement activities particularly difficult to conduct in an efficient manner," the office said. "The porous nature of the borders in West and Central Africa is a major factor of insecurity: the borders are neither demarcated or sufficiently controlled."

noticias.titulo: Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era
noticias.resumen: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.
noticias.texto:
Thawing of relations: Hungary and Ukraine turn a new page
November 25, 2026
The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.
One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.
Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.
Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.
For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.
Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."
Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."
From low point to fresh start
The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.
The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.
Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.
Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.
Closer economic cooperation
During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.
The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.
Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.
At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.
Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.
Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.
Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.
A fresh — but not always smooth — start
One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."
Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.
In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.
Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.
Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.
Hungarian attitudes to Ukraine
Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.
According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.
That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.
"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."
Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.
After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.
Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.
'Historic' meeting
Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."
He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."
A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.
The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.
Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.
A path forward
Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics (IEP) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."
No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.
Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.
Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."
This article was originally published in German.

noticias.titulo: Spain: Canary Islands witness 1-day migration record
noticias.resumen: The arrival of over 2,000 migrants to the islands comes as Spain holds elections this weekend. The president of the Canary Islands said the archipelago is facing "unprecedented migration pressure."
noticias.texto:
Spain: Canary Islands witness 1-day migration record
November 25, 2026
The Spanish Canary Islands witnessed a one-day migration record on Tuesday, with over 2,100 people arriving to the region in over 24 hours.
Most of the migrants landed on the the island of El Hierro, according to Spanish authorities.
'The Canaries can't take it anymore,' regional leader says
"The Canaries can't take it anymore. We're experiencing an unprecedented migration pressure," President of the Canary Islands Fernando Clavijo wrote on X. He requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss an immediate EU response.
Around 100 minors arrived on Tuesday, with a baby also born during the trip from Africa to the islands.
The Canaries, a tourist destination whose shortest gap with northwest Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), tends to see more migrant arrivals in the fall when the waters are calmer. The waters become rougher in the winter due to storms and swells.
Earlier this month, nearly 1,600 migrants from West Africa were saved and taken to the Canary Islands in a previous record. Over 26,000 migrants came to the Canaries this year so far — with half of that figure in November alone.
The route from Africa to the Canaries is one of the deadliest in the world for migrants.
Boats taking off for the islands sometimes drift out to open sea, with the migrants onboard facing starvation, dehydration and lack of medical care. Human smugglers frequently organize the trips and abuse the migrants.
Migration major topic as Spain holds snap vote Sunday
The spike in migration to the Canaries comes as Spain will hold a snap election on Sunday.
Migration, along with housing, will be one of the topics at the forefront of voters' minds when they cast their ballots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who belongs to the center-left Socialist Party, has faced backlash from the opposition regarding his tolerant attitude towards migration. The Spanish government earlier this year enacted a plan to legalize up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.
In late July, over 80,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta, triggering a crisis for the Sanchez government. Countries such as Germany and Italy tightened or extended border controls due to the influx of migrants into Ceuta.
The far-right Vox party, which could receive its best-ever result in upcoming election, has called for Sanchez and his ministers to be prosecuted for treason over the Ceuta crisis. The conservative Popular Party could form a coalition government with Vox after the election.

noticias.titulo: At this Little Free Bakery in Austin, neighbors come for the pastries and stay for community connection
noticias.resumen: The bakers behind these pop-up pastry drops aren't raking in the profits, but they are building a space for people to come together in polarized times.
noticias.texto:
At this Little Free Bakery in Austin, neighbors come for the pastries and stay for community connection
AUSTIN, Texas— When lines form in parks they're usually for the playground. Kids taking turns on slides. Runners waiting to get a drink from a water fountain. But the line that forms in the Bruning Green park in Austin's North Loop neighborhood happens only once a month, always on the first Sunday, and includes people of all ages. They're all here for Sarah Mason's bakery.
Unlike other bakeries in town where a pastry can run upwards of $7, everything here is free.
Mason's popup is one of countless Little Free Bakeries across the country. The idea is similar to Little Free Libraries, the small boxes that are often set up in front yards where passersby can leave or take a book as they please. Instead of books, it's baked goods that are up for grabs.
The bakers behind these Little Free Bakeries make everything from classic chocolate chip cookies to croissants all at no cost to their neighbors. Some have different reasons for starting than others, but what many inadvertently created is a space for their community to come together and get to know one another.
Mason started the Free Bakery North Loop last September when she was working on improving her technical pastry skills. She was handing out baked goods at her job as an office leasing representative for WeWork, but soon she had more than she could give away.
For her first free bakery, Mason made around 150 items, ranging from coconut chocolate chip cookies to bacon cheddar chive scones.
She thought people would happen upon the event as they were walking through the neighborhood. But just in case, she posted on social media. That post took off and since then there has always been a line.
"I have a friend who jokes that waiting in the line is the most fun part, because everyone's excited and talking about what they're going to get when they get to the front of the line and you can meet people," Mason said.
People love a free treat, but Mason said she is pleasantly surprised at how many people stick around and hang out.
"It was unexpected," she said. "My observation of other free bakeries, it's more of a grab and go situation. But because we were in this park, it felt like there was room to spread out and room for other activities. It became more of a community event than just a free pastry."
For people like Sara and J.R. Almanza, the event hearkens back to old Austin, a time before the tech boom when the skyline had fewer skyscrapers and when the pace of life felt slower and it was easier to strike up a conversation with strangers. After attending the free bakery once, the Almanzas decided to come back and enjoy the sense of community.
"Right now it seems like people are becoming more divided. It feels like everything's so polarizing these days," J.R. said. "There's so much out there to kind of distract us from meeting people and engaging with other people, that events like this are important because it brings people together."
That sense of community is part of what led Lanne Stauffer to create the very first Little Free Bakery in Seattle in 2021.
It all started in Seattle
Stauffer got the idea for a Little Free Bakery after she experienced a small act of kindness.
"We were still in the pandemic and the mood was scared and nobody was coming out of their houses and just a lot of fear in the air and there was a bouquet of flowers on my front step," Stauffer said.
Receiving those flowers created a shift in how she was feeling inside.
"Just the joy of finding that bouquet of flowers on my front step changed my day and I wanted to know what I could do to change other folks' day in the same way," she said.
But Stauffer isn't a florist. She's a baker. She thought of Little Free Libraries and asked her husband to build her a pick-up box.
"It gives me so much joy to bake for people," she said. "It's the way I say I love you, and so even if nobody came that day, just knowing I was baking for the community made me feel good."
That Tuesday, people did come though — and in an hour all 50 little apple pies were gone. By the time it was over, Stauffer decided she would do it again the following week.
It's been five years since then, and Stauffer has noticed a couple of things. Chocolate and lemon sweets are more popular than others. And the treats aren't the only reason people stop by.
"People are always grateful to have a place to come and meet their neighbors and have conversations often about what's going on in the news," she said. "We stand around and hug each other or laugh or cry, share our fears, and it's just added another gathering spot in our neighborhood."
Some neighbors even plan their weeks around the pastry drops.
Erin Creighton Tozier has lived in Seattle's Magnolia neighborhood for five years, but didn't know about the Stauffer's Little Free Bakery until a year ago.
"It's just like the anchor in our week," Creighton Tozier said. "I have a demanding job, but it's like a 3 p.m. calendar marker … a break in the day to get some fresh air. Even if it's raining, no matter the weather, like my dog and I go, we have a sweet treat, we chat with our neighbors."
To celebrate her neighbors coming out for five years, Stauffer baked a 5-foot-long white cake, with orange curd filling, a cardamom cream cheese frosting and a pomegranate molasses drizzle.
Her family helped decorate it with fall fruits before they put it out in the driveway.
"I have learned that folks need to feel connected and they can feel comforted by me just baking them something," she said.
The growing free bakery movement
It only took a couple months after Stauffer started the Little Free Bakery Seattle for another one to open up.
"Then it started to snowball from there, and I was having somebody reach out to me every month for a while opening a new little free bakery," Stauffer said. "I didn't know that I was starting a movement but that has been one of the biggest delights."
Now little free bakeries exist in Nashville, Tenn.; Salt Lake City, Utah; Fredericksburg, Va. and other cities.
Stauffer recently took a road trip to visit some of the other bakeries and collect stories and recipes from her fellow bakers for an upcoming book, The Little Free Bakery Book: Recipes for Sharing & Building Community, written with Jill Lightner.
Stauffer, like Mason in Austin, hopes that the movement continues to grow. "I think every neighborhood should have a little free bakery," Mason said.
In Austin, other free bakeries have popped up since Mason started hers. But the reach goes farther. In Chattanooga, Tenn., her sister plans to start a free bakery there.
"I think she just saw how much fun we're having here and thought that she wants a little slice of that in her own neighborhood," Mason said.

noticias.titulo: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
noticias.resumen: Several Democratic senators have been signaling this move, saying the party needs to acknowledge the diverse class of incoming freshman that catapulted the party to victory in November.
noticias.texto:
Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.
"The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter said. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal."
The letter, first reported by Politico, is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.
The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.
"These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."
Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.
"On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms.
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW that leadership extends beyond the top post.
"This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking issues, I want to see them running on the field."
The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader.
Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.
"Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.
On Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've said, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people."

noticias.titulo: Wrongly deported Salvadoran arrives in Spain after US legal battle
noticias.resumen: The Salvadoran, deported "by mistake" to a prison in El Salvador in 2025, has brought an end to 20 months of litigation in the United States, with Madrid as the first stop in what his lawyers describe as a temporary stay abroad.
noticias.texto:
The Salvadoran, deported "by mistake" to a prison in El Salvador in 2025, has brought an end to 20 months of litigation in the United States, with Madrid as the first stop in what his lawyers describe as a temporary stay abroad.
Kilmar Abrego García, a Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation from the United States put him at the centre of a controversy over US President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday.
His case became a focal point in the debate over Trump's mass deportation policy in 2025, raising concerns about migrants' rights to challenge deportation orders and the administration's compliance with court rulings.
Wearing sunglasses and a baseball cap, Abrego García made his way to a vehicle at Madrid airport without speaking to reporters gathered at the scene, according to AFP journalists.
"While details remain private, Kilmar is planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries," We Are CASA, a US immigrant advocacy group which has been supporting him, said in a statement.
The Salvadoran ultimately left the United States voluntarily on a commercial flight bound for Spain.
"I am leaving happy, I am leaving with my freedom," he said in a statement released by We Are CASA.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed his departure from the country in a statement, in which it labelled Abrego García a "trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator."
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, quoted in the statement.
His lawyers, for their part, welcomed the fact that their client had been able to leave "on his own terms" after his long-running dispute with the US immigration authorities.
One of his legal representatives, Simón Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the departure brought an end to a deportation campaign he described as "retaliation". He also stressed that the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego García, who is married to a US citizen, hopes to return to the United States once Donald Trump leaves the White House.
Deported "by mistake" to Bukele's mega-prison
His case began in March 2025, when federal agents arrested Abrego García in the street. Days later he was deported to El Salvador and sent to the Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), a controversial maximum-security mega-prison built on the orders of President Nayib Bukele and intended to house alleged members of criminal gangs.
The deportation went ahead even though there was a court order expressly prohibiting his deportation to El Salvador, where he had received threats from armed groups before leaving the country. The US government itself later acknowledged that it had been "a mistake", although it initially resisted facilitating his return.
Back in the United States, Abrego García reported having suffered beatings, sleep deprivation and psychological torture during the almost three months he was held in CECOT.
The legal battle reached the US Supreme Court, which ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. The authorities eventually brought him back to the country, although they did so in the context of a criminal investigation that led to an indictment over his alleged involvement in a migrant-smuggling network.
However, a federal judge ultimately dismissed all the charges, ruling that the indictment was in fact motivated by a desire to retaliate against the Salvadoran for having opposed his deportation.
The Trump administration tried to deport him to Africa
As the criminal case progressed, the US government continued trying to deport him from the country. The authorities considered sending him to Uganda, Ghana and Eswatini, but failed to secure agreement from those countries to receive him. Meanwhile, Abrego García applied for asylum to prevent his deportation.
The dispute became one of the most high-profile cases under Trump's immigration policy and highlighted the differences between the executive and judicial branches over the limits of presidential powers regarding deportations.
Throughout the process, the US president and several members of his administration publicly accused the Salvadoran of belonging to Mara Salvatrucha, also known as MS-13, as well as of human trafficking and assaulting his wife, all allegations that were echoed in the statement published on Tuesday by the DHS announcing his departure from the country.
However, these accusations were called into question by the courts. In fact, federal judge Paula Xinis, who oversaw part of the litigation in Maryland, went so far as to open a contempt-of-court inquiry against some of the prosecutors involved in the case for allegedly repeatedly disobeying her orders.
Now, with Madrid as his first stop, Abrego García plans to travel to other countries to take part in various events and speak about his experience, according to Sandoval-Moshenberg.

noticias.titulo: At least 30 killed in highway fire in Cairo district
noticias.resumen: A truck carrying fuel reportedly overturned on a busy highway, setting vehicles ablaze and prompting a major emergency response. Authorities warned that the death toll could rise.
noticias.texto:
A truck carrying fuel reportedly overturned on a busy highway, setting vehicles ablaze and prompting a major emergency response. Authorities warned that the death toll could rise.
At least 30 people were killed and 15 others injured after a fire broke out on a major highway in the Egyptian capital Cairo on Wednesday, the country's Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said.
The blaze erupted after a truck carrying fuel overturned on a busy highway, according to Egyptian state media.
Footage captured by passers-by showed a massive blaze and thick clouds of smoke rising from the scene.
Emergency workers pulled people from burning vehicles as firefighters battled the flames. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a suburb of Cairo.
Abdel Ghaffar said 39 ambulances were dispatched to the scene, with 15 injured people taken to hospital.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement.
The Health Minister said he would visit the scene, adding that the death toll was preliminary and could rise further.
Traffic accidents claim thousands of lives in Egypt every year, with speeding, poor road conditions and inadequate enforcement of traffic laws among the leading causes of crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 others injured in a multi-vehicle collision on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

noticias.titulo: French judo legend and Olympic medalist Teddy Riner says Ukraine is not France's war
noticias.resumen: Five months ahead of France's presidential elections, the question of support to Ukraine has become a major campaign topic.
noticias.texto:
Five months ahead of France's presidential elections, the question of support to Ukraine has become a major campaign topic.
Five time French Olympic gold medallist and presidential candidate Teddy Riner declared on Wednesday that he did "not understand" why France was sending troops to Ukraine.
Speaking on the sidelines of a mayoral congress in Paris, he said that the fact that troops had been sent to Ukraine without public prior knowledge "smelled bad."
When questioned about France's solidarity with Ukraine, given it is part of the European continent, he responded "is Ukraine in the European Union?"
"If tomorrow I become president, I will strive to be the person who unites people and makes them join hands", he added.
Riner's comments come more than a week after a source disclosed to French media that foreign soldiers had been deployed on a secret training mission in Ukraine for several months to train personnel and help maintain equipment.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov subsequently told reporters during a press conference that this amounted to "direct participation in the war, including target designation assistance, satellite data provision, and other forms of support."
France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot subsequently denied allegations of direct involvement, underlining that the country was not involved in a military operation, but in "training and maintenance, carried out far from the front lines, with very limited scope and no involvement in warfare".
In early November, the European Council extended Europe's Military Assistance Mission to Ukraine for a further two years. This EU framework provides non-executive military training, mentoring, and advisory support to partner armed forces.
According to a poll published by Elabe on 14 November, Teddy Riner is polling around 4.5%, trailing far behind the hard-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen and the Jean Luc Mélenchon's hard-left France Unbowed party.

noticias.titulo: Greece: 14,000 march in Athens against rising living costs
noticias.resumen: Thousands demonstrated across Greece on Wednesday 25 November 2026 during a 24-hour strike against rising living costs and stagnant wages. The industrial action disrupted metro services, grounded flights and kept ferries in port.
noticias.texto:
Around 14,000 people took to the streets of Athens and Thessaloniki, according to police, in response to strike calls by unions representing civil servants, dockworkers and teachers. In the capital, demonstrators carrying banners and red flags gathered outside the Greek parliament, chanting slogans under the watch of riot police. The industrial action disrupted Athens metro services, kept ferries in port and grounded flights to and from 15 regional airports. Workers, students and pensioners demanded higher wages, better working conditions and improved public services as rising living costs continued to erode their purchasing power.
Although Greece's economy is forecast to grow by 1.8% this year, outpacing the eurozone average of 1.1%, many households are struggling to make ends meet. The gross monthly minimum wage stands at €968, while housing costs and rents have soared in the wake of the post-pandemic tourism boom. Annual inflation reached 5.7% in October, according to the national statistics authority, Elstat. The civil servants' union ADEDY condemned stagnant wages, energy insecurity and deteriorating public healthcare and education services. Conservative prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, who is seeking a third term in next year's election, has pledged to raise the minimum wage to €1,000 in early 2028 if re-elected.

noticias.titulo: Bring the noise: Meet the young Italians ringing church bells to protect the past
noticias.resumen: Across northern Italy, a new generation is keeping the centuries-old art of church bell ringing alive. As automated systems replace traditional techniques, young enthusiasts are learning to play the bells by hand, combining precision, teamwork and improvisation.
noticias.texto:
Across northern Italy, a new generation is keeping the centuries-old art of church bell ringing alive. As automated systems replace traditional techniques, young enthusiasts are learning to play the bells by hand, combining precision, teamwork and improvisation.
In northern Italy, a new generation is keeping the centuries-old art of manual church bell ringing alive, resisting the spread of automated systems.
At the Church of Saint Martin the Bishop in Bellusco, young enthusiasts pull heavy ropes to produce the melodies that once echoed from church towers across the region.
Today, church bells are increasingly operated electronically. For Corrado Codazza, president of the Federation of Ambrosian Bell Ringers, the preservation of the tradition is also about recognising bells as musical instruments and protecting a cultural heritage that was once close to disappearing.
But members of the Federation are determined to preserve the traditional craft, bringing together several dozen enthusiasts, more than half of them under the age of 30.
The tradition requires more than physical strength. Bell ringers must master timing, coordination and the ability to follow a conductor, much like musicians in an orchestra. Learning the craft is a hands-on process. Training takes place inside the bell tower, where enthusiasts gradually develop the technique needed to control the instruments.
“You start knowing little to nothing, perhaps having watched a few videos online to get an idea of what it’s like, before stepping into the world of manual bell ringing,” says 21-year-old Simone Malinverno.
Performances are also an opportunity to bring creativity back into the tradition. Unlike automated systems, which repeat the same sequences, manual bell ringing allows conductors to introduce variations and improvise.
The art of bell ringing was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in December 2024, giving further international recognition to the efforts of those working to preserve it.
“I like to think that people notice when the bell tower is playing something different," says 28-year-old computer programmer Alessandro Dameno. "While an automated system always delivers the exact same rendition, a manual performance incorporates the inventiveness of the conductor, who may call upon the bells in a different sequence, ensuring there is always something new. No two performances are ever the same,” he adds.
The group also hopes to restore manual bell ringing in places where the practice has disappeared, creating opportunities for new performances and passing the skills on to future generations.

noticias.titulo: Socialists and Liberals suspend coalition talks after EPP again sides with far right
noticias.resumen: The three centrist groups had been negotiating a coalition for the second half of the European Parliament's term, including a joint push to secure Roberta Metsola's re-election as president.
noticias.texto:
The three centrist groups had been negotiating a coalition for the second half of the European Parliament's term, including a joint push to secure Roberta Metsola's re-election as president.
The Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and the liberal Renew Europe groups in the European Parliament suspended coalition talks with the conservative European People's Party (EPP) on Wednesday, parliamentary sources familiar with the matter told Euronews.
The move followed the centre-right EPP’s decision to join forces with far-right groups to pass a revision of environmental assessment rules, a strategy it has repeatedly employed during the current parliamentary term.
The EPP, S&D and Renew make up the centrist majority supporting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Their leaders, Manfred Weber, Iratxe García Pérez and Valérie Hayer, were due to negotiate a cooperation agreement for the second half of Parliament’s term, including a deal on Roberta Metsola’s re-election as parliament president next January.
The EPP clashed with its traditional partners on legislation called "Omnibus VIII", proposed by the European Commission to speed up environmental assessments. The centre-right group privileged simplification over environmental safeguards and turned to the far right after it could not clinch a deal with S&D and Renew, which supported the inclusion of more safeguards in the legislation.
The coalition agreement would also outline shared legislative priorities and working arrangements, although negotiations remain difficult.
S&D and Renew are demanding a written EPP commitment to stop voting with the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), the far right Patriots for Europe (PfE) and Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN).
The main sticking point of the negotiations is how to prevent the EPP from joining forces with the far right. EPP leader Manfred Weber ushered in a right-wing majority during the current parliamentary term by backing legislation on environmental and migration issues alongside the ECR, PfE and ESN.
Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Weber stopped short of committing to an agreement that would oblige the EPP to consistently vote alongside its centrist partners.
All negotiations on the coalition agreement for the second part of the legislaturehave been suspended until further notice. Parliamentary sources say the Socialists and Liberals are demanding “strong safeguards” in the agreement to prevent a repeat of the episode.
Sources within Renew Europe say the group regards a written agreement as a prerequisite for supporting Metsola’s re-election.
